evidence.text: [Synthetic fixture text; not from the cited article.] Section 4.2, illustrative. Language-model assistants are increasingly asked to draft procedures, summarise prior results, and propose candidate explanations for laboratory observations. A recurring difficulty is that a language model may return a fluent answer that reads as credible yet states something false. A second difficulty is that the explanation a model writes for its answer need not describe the steps that actually produced it, so a convincing rationale can hide an unreliable process. Both problems matter more in experimental science than in casual use, because a wrong suggestion can cost materials, instrument time, and the trust of the people reviewing the work. Grounding the model in curated reference material is proposed here as a practical way to reduce both problems. Supplying the model with vetted domain material, whether through instructions, retrieved passages, or additional training, gives reviewers a concrete way to check its claims and makes such errors less frequent. Pairing such grounding with inspection of the model's internal behaviour is treated as a direction worth testing rather than an established result, and the synthetic study reports no measurements for it.

[Synthetic fixture text; not from the cited article.] Section 5.1, illustrative. The synthetic survey compares two ways of bringing domain knowledge into automated analysis. The first adapts a general-purpose language model by adding instructions, retrieved reference passages, or a short round of additional training on vetted examples. The second relies on compact task-specific models whose predictions are checked against curated reference data before they are reported. Compact models are cheaper to run and easier to audit, but each one covers only a narrow task, while a general model covers many tasks but is harder to verify. The survey does not rank the two approaches; it argues that the choice depends on how costly an undetected error would be in a given setting. dimension_summaries.summary: The papers address supporting and evaluating LLM capabilities in scientific hypothesis generation, domain-specific constitutive modeling, and establishing systematic frameworks or surveys across stages of scientific discovery.
Methodologies range from multi-module feedback frameworks and bilevel parameter optimization to surveys categorizing knowledge-injection strategies and LLM roles across scientific stages.
Evaluated datasets include manually annotated social science literature, bibliographic and chemical databases, synthetic multiaxial testing data, and specialized idea generation benchmarks.
LLMs demonstrate effectiveness in proposing novel and valid hypotheses, accelerating literature synthesis, and achieving high precision when augmented with domain-specific theory and feedback.
Primary reported limitations are model hallucinations, unfaithful reasoning/explanations, reliance on domain-specific theory to achieve accuracy, and constrained domain coverage or dataset sizes.

Future directions emphasize advancing physics-infused and causal AI, incorporating knowledge graphs to capture tail knowledge, extending coverage to social sciences, and building agent workflows whose explanations can be audited.

gaps.title: Integrating Knowledge Graphs into LLM-Based Hypothesis Generation to Preserve Tail Knowledge
gaps.description: While LLM-based agent frameworks (e.g., SciAgents, KG-CoI) use academic knowledge graphs for research idea generation, standard models still struggle to retain low-frequency domain facts wiped out during general pre-training. Frameworks specifically designed to curate and dynamically query theme-focused knowledge graphs to preserve fine-grained tail knowledge during LLM hypothesis generation remain underexplored.

Cross-referencing these findings indicates a missing integration between graph-structured domain knowledge bases and generative hypothesis loops.

gaps.title: Cross-Disciplinary Generalizability and Evaluation of Hypothesis Generation Frameworks Across Natural and Social Sciences
gaps.description: Current research frameworks and surveys tend to either focus strictly on social sciences or omit social sciences entirely in favor of natural sciences and mathematics, leaving the cross-disciplinary generalizability of LLM hypothesis generation techniques unverified within this corpus.
gaps.reasoning: P1 evaluates hypothesis generation using annotated social science literature, while P2 explicitly acknowledges omitting social sciences due to scope limits. gaps.confidence_reason: Directly supported by limitation and scope statements in P1-E3 and P2-E4 across distinct paper contexts.
gaps.research_opportunity: Researchers might explore benchmark datasets and comparative evaluations to test whether feedback mechanisms established in social sciences translate effectively to natural science discovery tasks.

gaps.title: Faithful Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation in Autonomous Scientific Discovery Agents
gaps.description: LLMs deployed for scientific discovery frequently exhibit unfaithful reasoning and generate plausible but incorrect hypotheses, creating a gap between generation capabilities and trustworthy self-explanation.
gaps.reasoning: P4 identifies hallucinations and unfaithful explanations as key limitations in scientific agent workflows, while P5 emphasizes that general LLMs without rigorous knowledge injection struggle with precision and factual accuracy. Together, they highlight a methodological gap in ensuring faithful reasoning in automated research agents.
gaps.evidence_summary: P4-E4 identifies model hallucinations and unfaithful reasoning as key limitations, and P5-E1 reports that unaugmented LLMs lack precision and exhibit accuracy constraints on specialized tasks.
gaps.confidence_reason: Supported by consistent limitation reports across P4-E4 and P5-E1 regarding LLM hallucinations and unfaithful self-explanations. (Capped at medium: fewer than 3 supporting papers.)
gaps.research_opportunity: Investigating self-verification mechanisms and explainable agent architectures could potentially improve the faithfulness and accuracy of LLM-generated scientific explanations.

gaps.title: Synthesizing Multi-Module Feedback Prompting with Quantitative Physics and Theoretical Constraints
gaps.description: Existing frameworks apply either qualitative discrete prompting feedback (e.g., novelty/clarity) or quantitative parameter optimization against mathematical domain equations, but lack unified methods that combine multi-criteria qualitative feedback with strict quantitative domain optimization.
gaps.reasoning: Comparing P1 (which utilizes multi-module qualitative feedback loops for novelty, reality, and clarity) with P3 (which enforces physical constitutive equations via bilevel parameter optimization) highlights an underexplored opportunity to unify discrete qualitative multi-criteria feedback with rigorous numeric domain optimization.
